catalog_quote: As shown in the data given in this thesis thus far, stress in SQ is most commonly penultimate. In this section stress will be examined, since there are some occasions when the penultimate syllable stress pattern is apparently broken. [...] The above two syllable words all receive penultimate stress whether their first syllable is V, CV, or CVC. This is true of monomorphemic three and four syllable words also, although my corpus contains few examples. [...] The stress of inflected verbs is always penultimate. [...] Inflected nouns exhibit the same stress pattern as above. [p. 51] Some morphemes such as /=ga/ (Topic Marker) that occur postpositionally occur in two different patterns: one where penultimate stress is assigned as if /=ga/ were not part of the word, and another where stress is assigned as if /=ga/ were part of the word. [p. 52] SQ puts primary stress on the last syllable of a focused element in yes-no questions, which overrides any other primary stress on this element. [p. 55] Secondary stress occurs on every second syllable to the left of the primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (inflected) word regardless of syllable shape; certain postposed elements (=ga topic, =da accusative, =mi affirmative, -lla 'just', =chu Y/N) are optionally outside the stress domain, so stress may appear antepenultimate on the surface string when they are not cliticized.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of the primary stress (p. 55, ex. 92 /ˌtawga riGˌsiSka-ˈguna/); apparent secondary stress to the right of primary before =ma is analysed as phrasal.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Postposed =ga, =da, =mi, -lla optionally cliticize: ['wataza] ~ [wa'taza] 'just a year' (sec. 5.2, pp. 51-52); (ii) a focused element in yes-no questions takes primary stress on its LAST syllable, overriding penultimate stress (pp. 52-53); (iii) contractions often keep stress on the syllable it would have had without contraction, yielding surface final stress, though penultimate is also possible (p. 53, exx. 86-87); (iv) =ma 'certainly' behaves as a separate word for stress (pp. 54-56).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including inflectional suffixes; some enclitics optionally excluded. Final stress is a phrase-level focus device in yes-no questions. Data are the author's SIL fieldwork in Salasaca, Tungurahua.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Salasaca Quichua (SQ), spoken in Salasaca parish, Tungurahua province, Ecuador — the variety Glottolog files under sala1272 'Tungurahua Highland Quichua' / ISO qxl (Salasaca Highland Quichua). No dialect mismatch.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Stress' (pp. 49-56): stress in SQ is most commonly penultimate; inflected verbs and nouns always penultimate; postposed =ga, =da, =mi, -lla (and =chu) optionally cliticize so stress may fall as if they were outside the word; focused element in yes-no questions gets final primary stress; contractions may keep stress on original syllable; secondary stress on every second syllable to the left of primary; =ma treated as separate word on stress evidence.

tone.quote: This thesis investigates the prosodic system of Salasaka Kichwa, focusing on the interaction between pitch, morphosyntactic structure, and word order in both elicited and spontaneous speech. Based on data from ten native speakers of the Salasaka community, the study analyzes approximately 150 utterances using Praat and ToBI-style prosodic annotation. The findings reveal a consistent alignment between the nuclear pitch accent and the leftmost constituent of the verb phrase in neutral declarative sentences [...]. This default prosodic alignment is disrupted by the presence of focus-sensitive or interrogative morphemes such as -mi and -chu, which reliably attract the pitch peak regardless of their position in the clause.

tone.quote: Stress. With few exceptions, such as the onomatopoeic noun /guˈlun/ 'thunder', the penultimate syllable of the word receives the primary stress. The exceptions include words with the comitative/instrumental suffix /-n/ in which the stress always falls on the last syllable: /ˈindi/ 'sun', /inˈdin/ 'with the sun', /ˈtʃaki/ 'foot', /tʃaˈkin/ 'with the foot'. This suffix is presumably a reduction of the suffix /-wan/ which continues to be used in more formal speech styles.

tone.quote: 3. Acento. Con muy pocas excepciones, como el sustantivo onomatopéyico /ɡuˈlun/ 'trueno', se acentúa la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. Las excepciones incluyen palabras con el sufijo comitativo/instrumental /–n/ en que el acento siempre se presenta en la última sílaba: /ˈindi/ 'sol', /inˈdin/ 'con el sol', /ˈʧɑki/ 'pie', /ʧɑˈkin/ 'con el pie'.
tone.translation: 3. Stress. With very few exceptions, such as the onomatopoeic noun /guˈlun/ 'thunder', the penultimate syllable of the word is stressed. The exceptions include words with the comitative/instrumental suffix /-n/, in which stress always occurs on the last syllable: 'sun', 'with the sun', 'foot', 'with the foot'.
